subject: Communication
title: Nonverbal Leakage: When the Body Betrays You
description: Learn Nonverbal Leakage: When the Body Betrays You in one minute.

hook.text: A CEO announces record earnings with a smile — but her foot is tapping and her hands grip the podium.

buildup.text: Nonverbal leakage occurs when true emotions seep through despite attempts to control body language.

discovery.text: We manage our faces well, but extremities — feet, hands, neck — are harder to control consciously.

twist.text: The further a body part is from the face, the more honest it tends to be. Feet are the most reliable.

climax.text: FBI interrogators watch feet and hands, not faces, because those are the channels people forget to manage.

punchline.text: Your face lies best. Your feet tell the truth.

quiz.question: Which body parts are most likely to show nonverbal leakage?

details.summary: Nonverbal leakage occurs when true emotions escape through body language despite attempts to conceal them. Feet shifting, micro-gestures, and voice changes reveal what words try to hide.
details.whyItMatters: Recognizing leakage cues helps detect emotional truth in high-stakes conversations where people are motivated to mask their real feelings.
takeaways: The body leaks emotions that the face tries to conceal
Lower body signals like feet movement are hardest to control
Leakage increases under cognitive load and stress

faq.question: Which body parts leak emotions most reliably?
faq.answer: The feet and legs are the most reliable leakage sites because people focus on controlling their face and forget their lower body. Foot tapping, ankle locking, and orienting feet toward exits often reveal concealed anxiety or desire to leave.

faq.question: Is nonverbal leakage the same as lying tells?
faq.answer: Not exactly. Leakage reveals concealed emotions, which may or may not involve deception. Someone may suppress excitement about a gift they already know about or hide sadness to appear strong. Context determines whether leakage indicates a lie.
